overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Merleau-Ponty's account of other people. You'll be asked about cultural objects, the argument from analogy, the infant example, intercorporeality, and the limits of access to others.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Walking a worn path through a field, you sense that people have walked here before. How does Merleau-Ponty describe the path?

options.html: As a physical object from which you infer past walkers
options.text: As a physical object from which you infer past walkers
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The path isn't an object you reason from. It's a cultural object in which others are anonymously present.

options.html: As a cultural object in which others are present
options.text: As a cultural object in which others are present
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Cultural objects bear the traces of human action, and others are present in them as an anonymous "someone."

options.html: As a memory of other people you've seen walking
options.text: As a memory of other people you've seen walking
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The presence of others in the path isn't a memory. It's part of how the path is perceived.

options.html: As evidence that the field is private property
options.text: As evidence that the field is private property
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The point is that the path is a cultural object, bearing the anonymous presence of others.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Merleau-Ponty say the argument from analogy can't even get started?

options.html: Because other people's behavior is too varied to compare
options.text: Because other people's behavior is too varied to compare
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The problem is more basic: I don't perceive my own expressions as I perceive others'.

options.html: Because I don't see my own expressions as I see others'
options.text: Because I don't see my own expressions as I see others'
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! I feel my anger from within and see the other's from without, so there's nothing to compare.

options.html: Because animals behave like us without having minds
options.text: Because animals behave like us without having minds
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The argument's problem is that my inner experience and the other's outer appearance can't be compared.

options.html: Because analogies are never valid forms of reasoning
options.text: Because analogies are never valid forms of reasoning
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty's point is specific: there's no basis for comparing my expressions with others'.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following fit Merleau-Ponty's account of how we perceive others? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: One body-subject responds directly to another
options.text: One body-subject responds directly to another

options.html: My body schema lets me perceive others' bodily intentions
options.text: My body schema lets me perceive others' bodily intentions
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The infant perceives the adult's jaws through its own body schema.

options.html: The other's experience, as lived, is never fully mine
options.text: The other's experience, as lived, is never fully mine

options.html: I infer the other's mind by comparing it with my own
options.text: I infer the other's mind by comparing it with my own
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the argument from analogy, which Merleau-Ponty rejects.

options.html: Others are hidden minds reached only by theory
options.text: Others are hidden minds reached only by theory
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. For Merleau-Ponty, others are partly visible in their conduct.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's later term, from "The Philosopher and His Shadow," for the relation between body-subjects in which one lived body perceives and responds to another directly? Enter one word.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Intercorporeality names the shared bodily life in which others are perceived.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty's later term is intercorporeality.

forms.stemHtml: Why does the infant's response to the pretend bite count against the argument from analogy?

options.html: Because infants reason more quickly than adults do
options.text: Because infants reason more quickly than adults do
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The point is that the infant has no image of its own biting jaws to compare with.

options.html: Because the infant later learns to imitate on purpose
options.text: Because the infant later learns to imitate on purpose
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The point is that the infant can't compare the adult's jaws with an image of its own.

options.html: Because it has no image of its own jaws to compare
options.text: Because it has no image of its own jaws to compare
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Having hardly seen its own face, the infant can't be using analogy. It perceives the bite through its body schema.

options.html: Because newborns imitate facial gestures from birth
options.text: Because newborns imitate facial gestures from birth
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The example concerns a 15-month-old, and neonatal imitation is disputed. The point is the lack of a self-image.

title: Intercorporeality
